Baltimore by the numbers

Where is Baltimore, and why does it bill property tax differently from a county?

Baltimore sits in north-central Maryland on the Patapsco River, and it has been an independent city since 1851. It is almost entirely surrounded by Baltimore County but is politically separate from it, so there is no county tax bill layered on top of the city bill.

The city covers about 92 square miles, of which roughly 11 are water. Elevation runs from sea level at the harbor to around 480 feet in the northwest, which matters for older homes: lower blocks near the water see more flooding, while hillside neighborhoods deal more with drainage and old foundations.

For a seller, the practical point is simple. One city bill carries the city rate and the state rate together, and the same office that collects it also controls the annual tax sale. That makes a Baltimore tax balance a bigger deal than the same dollar amount in a county with a slower process.

What is the Baltimore property tax rate, and how is a bill calculated?

The city rate is $2.248 per $100 of assessed value, and the State of Maryland adds $0.112 per $100, collected on the same bill and forwarded to the state. Together that is $2.360 per $100, or $2,360 a year on each $100,000 of taxable assessment before credits.

The City of Baltimore says the state Department of Assessments and Taxation sets each parcel's value and the city multiplies its own rate by that figure. The city rate is also listed on the budget office's tax-rate page, which shows $2.248 for fiscal 2027. A 2024 news report described it as the highest rate in the state.

ItemWhat the sources say
City real property rate$2.248 per $100 of assessed value
State rate on the city bill$0.112 per $100
Combined$2.360 per $100 (sum of the two rates)
Homestead credit cap, from July 1, 20264% a year on a principal residence
City transfer tax1.5% of the cash consideration
Recordation tax$5.00 per $500 of consideration paid

The transfer and recordation taxes have a reduced yield on sales over $1 million, and part of each goes to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. Who pays them at closing is a contract term, so check your sales contract.

How did the 2026 reassessment affect Baltimore homes?

Baltimore was in Maryland's Group 2 reassessment, and residential full cash value rose 13.4% between January 1, 2023 and January 1, 2026. Statewide, Group 2 residential values rose 13.2%, so the city landed close to the state figure.

Notices went out on December 30, 2025. Increases are phased in evenly over three years, while decreases take effect in full in the 2026 tax year. Owners who live in the home and have applied for the homestead credit are protected by the 4% cap, which means a large jump in market value does not translate into a large jump in the taxable figure right away.

If you inherited a house or moved out years ago, check whether the credit is still attached. It requires a principal residence, so a house that has become a rental or sits empty can lose the cap and see the taxable value catch up faster.

When are Baltimore tax bills mailed, and what happens if they go unpaid?

Bills are mailed July 1 and are due on receipt, with a half-percent discount if paid by July 31. After October 1, unpaid tax accrues 1% interest plus a 1% monthly penalty.

Owner-occupied homes and small businesses with taxes under $100,000 can pay in two equal installments, with a small fee added to the second. A pending appeal does not excuse a late payment, but a successful appeal produces a refund with interest.

A property becomes eligible for the annual tax sale once it is behind by at least $750 on an owner-occupied residence or $250 on a non-owner-occupied one. The city sends a final bill and legal notice in the first week of February, a second letter in the first week of April, and holds the online sale in May.

  • First week of February: Final Bill and Legal Notice mailed to the address in land records.
  • First week of April: second letter.
  • May: the annual tax sale.
  • First week of July: post-sale informational letter.

Owners can stop a sale by redeeming, which means paying the winning bidder all claims, interest and costs. The city also runs a Tax Sale Deferral Program through Finance and Housing and Community Development that can keep a property out of the sale for a year.

What other city charges can become a lien on a Baltimore house?

Unpaid annual registration fees for non-owner-occupied property are a lien and are subject to tax sale, according to the Department of Housing and Community Development. That catches many sellers by surprise, because the fees are small each year and easy to miss on a rental or a vacant house you inherited.

The housing department's information sheet lists the fee structure in effect at the time it was published:

  • 1- and 2-family dwellings: $30 per dwelling unit.
  • Multifamily dwellings: $35 per dwelling unit or $25 per rooming unit.
  • Vacant residential structures: $100 per structure plus $30 per dwelling unit.
  • Vacant lots: $25 per lot.

Owners of registered vacant buildings must keep them clean and secure until they are razed or rehabilitated, and the city bills the owner if it does the work first. As of mid-2024 the housing department reported 13,411 vacant building notices, 863 of them on city-owned property.

State law passed in 2024 also lets the City Council set a special tax rate on abandoned properties, effective June 1, 2024. The news report we read said no rate had been set at that time, so confirm with the city before assuming one applies to your property.

What is the economy and housing stock behind a Baltimore sale?

Johns Hopkins University and Johns Hopkins Hospital are the largest employers, and the city's gross domestic product was reported at about $62 billion in 2023. Other named employers include Under Armour, McCormick and T. Rowe Price. The port is another anchor, with a 2014 figure of 14,630 direct jobs.

Housing is dominated by rowhouses, many with brick or formstone fronts. The city has more than 65,000 buildings on the National Register of Historic Places, which is more than any other American city. Historic status can affect what exterior work you are allowed to do, so ask before you assume a quick cosmetic fix is permitted.

Population was 585,708 in the 2020 census and an estimated 569,997 for 2025, down from a peak of 949,708 in 1950. Neighborhoods named in the source include Canton, Fells Point, Federal Hill, Highlandtown, Roland Park and Pimlico, each with its own mix of owners and renters.

How do roads, rail and weather affect a Baltimore house?

Baltimore has a humid subtropical climate, with a July average near 80.7 degrees Fahrenheit and a January average near 35.8. Annual precipitation is about 45 inches at BWI and seasonal snowfall averages about 19 inches.

Hurricanes or their remnants can flood parts of downtown even though the city is not in a typical storm-surge zone. Buyers and inspectors look hard at basements, rear additions and roofs on rowhouses after a wet year.

Getting around is easier than in most Maryland places. Penn Station is among the nation's busiest rail stations, MARC runs three lines to Washington, Light RailLink runs from Hunt Valley to BWI, and Metro SubwayLink runs from downtown to Owings Mills. I-95 passes through the Fort McHenry Tunnel and I-83 is the Jones Falls Expressway. The Francis Scott Key Bridge on I-695 collapsed in March 2024.

What should a Baltimore seller with tax due do first?

Start by finding out what you owe and whether the property has been marked for the May sale. The collections call center is at 410-396-3000, and assessment questions and credits go to the state office at 410-767-8250.

  1. Pull the current bill on the city payment site and note any balance carried from earlier years.
  2. Check whether registration or other city charges are attached to the account.
  3. Ask for a payoff figure good through your expected closing date.
  4. Tell the title company early so the payoff is built into the settlement statement.

If money is tight, a payment plan or the deferral program may buy time. If the house needs work and the balance keeps growing, selling as-is for cash can be a cleaner way to clear the lien from the proceeds at closing.

More questions about Baltimore, MD Property Tax Guide

What is the Baltimore City property tax rate?

The city rate is $2.248 per $100 of assessed value, and the state adds $0.112 per $100 on the same bill. That is $2.360 combined, before any credits.

Does Baltimore property tax go up when my house is reassessed?

Not all at once for most owners. Increases are phased in over three years, and a principal residence with the homestead credit is capped at 4% a year from July 1, 2026. Baltimore's residential values rose 13.4% in the 2026 reassessment.

How much unpaid tax puts a Baltimore house into the tax sale?

The city says a property becomes eligible once it is delinquent by at least $750 for an owner-occupied residence or $250 for other property. The sale is held online each May after notices in February and April.

Can I sell a Baltimore house that is already in the tax sale process?

Usually yes, but timing matters. The city says owners can stop a sale by redeeming, so ask the collections office for a payoff figure and tell your title company right away.

Do unpaid rental registration fees affect a sale?

They can. The housing department states that unpaid registration fees are a lien against the property and subject to tax sale, so clear them before closing.

What are the Baltimore transfer and recordation taxes?

The city lists a transfer tax of 1.5% of the cash consideration and a recordation tax of $5.00 per $500 of consideration. Who pays each is negotiated in the contract.

Frederick by the numbers

Where is the city of Frederick, Maryland?

Frederick is the seat of Frederick County, about 46 miles west of Baltimore, 50 miles north and slightly west of Washington, D.C., and 24 miles southeast of Hagerstown. It sits at 341 feet of elevation and covers 24.56 square miles, almost all of it land.

Daniel Dulany laid out the town by 1745, and it became the county seat when Frederick County was formed in 1748. Schifferstadt, built in 1756, is probably the oldest surviving house in the city. Frederick was a stop on the Great Wagon Road and the National Road, a rail and canal hub in the 1830s, and the site of the 1864 Battle of Monocacy.

The city counted 78,171 people in 2020, and the 2025 estimate listed by Wikipedia is 92,059.

What is the layout of Frederick, and where are the older neighborhoods?

Frederick has a dense, walkable historic core surrounded by newer growth, and the core is where most of the preservation rules apply. Market, Patrick and East Streets carry more than 200 retailers, restaurants and antique shops in the Frederick Historic District, and downtown has about 600 businesses and organizations.

  • West Patrick Street follows the former National Road, now U.S. 40.
  • Monocacy Boulevard is a circular road that supports the core.
  • Culler Lake is a man-made lake downtown, and the church spires give the city its Clustered Spires nickname.
  • First Saturday draws about 11,000 people on average to downtown each month.

Wikipedia does not describe individual residential neighborhoods, so we do not name them here.

How do roads and transit shape the Frederick housing market?

Several major roads meet in Frederick: I-70, I-270, U.S. 15 and U.S. 340 meet here. I-70 runs east-west toward Baltimore and Hagerstown, I-270 runs southeast toward Washington, and U.S. 15 runs north toward Gettysburg.

ConnectionWhat it does
I-70East-west link to Baltimore and Hagerstown
I-270Spur toward Washington, D.C.
U.S. 15North-south toward Gettysburg, Pennsylvania
MARC commuter railRuns to Washington on former B&O lines
Express bus 991Goes to the Shady Grove Metro station
Frederick Municipal Airport (FDK)General aviation

Local TransIT buses and Greyhound also serve the city.

Who are the major employers in and around Frederick?

Fort Detrick is the largest employer in the Frederick area, with 10,827 employees in the 2025 figures reported by Wikipedia, and the county school board is next at 7,433. The list below shows the main public and institutional employers.

  • Frederick Health: 3,360
  • Frederick County Government: 2,810
  • Leidos Biomedical Research: 2,370
  • Frederick Community College: 1,369
  • City government: 977

Riverside Research Park, on the east side, hosts the National Cancer Institute's Frederick National Laboratory. Hood College and Frederick Community College are the city's higher education campuses, and Mount St. Mary's University has a campus in Frederick County.

What is the weather in Frederick, and what does it mean for a house?

Frederick has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and generally cool winters. The mean daily high is about 88.6 degrees in July and 43.1 degrees in January.

Average annual precipitation is 43.52 inches, and average snowfall is 16.5 inches. The state record high of 109 degrees was set in Frederick on July 10, 1936.

Flooding has a local history. The Carroll Creek flood control project began in the late 1970s to reduce flood risk to downtown from the 100-year floodplain. Its first phase, costing nearly $11 million, runs from Court Street to just past Carroll Street. The Carroll Creek Overlay District in the city code sets design standards for new construction and rehabilitation near the creek. The park along it includes brick paths, water features, pedestrian bridges and a 350-seat amphitheater, and Wikipedia reports more than $150 million in private investment underway or planned nearby, covering office, retail, residential and parking development.

What property tax rate applies inside the city of Frederick?

A house inside the city of Frederick had a combined real property rate of 1.7382 per $100 of assessed value in the fiscal 2025 state table, made of a county rate and a city rate. The table is published by the Department of Legislative Services from SDAT data.

Piece of the rate (fiscal 2025)Per $100 of assessed value
County rate in the city1.0077
Municipal rate0.7305
Combined1.7382
Unincorporated Frederick County, for comparison1.1100

The county's Treasury page says each municipality levies its own district tax for services like street maintenance, trash removal and police, and that homestead credit caps vary by municipality from 0 percent to 10 percent. We could not confirm from an official page whether the city portion appears on the county's bill, so ask the Treasury at 301-600-1111 before you pay.

What dates and appeal steps apply to a Frederick city owner?

Frederick County Treasury lists annual bills and the first installment as due September 30, with the second installment December 31, and interest of 1 percent per month starts October 1. Payments in July earn a 1 percent discount and August payments a one-half percent discount.

Assessments come from SDAT, which values property about every three years. An owner can appeal to the Supervisor of Assessments within 45 days of the notice date, to the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board within 30 days after that decision, and to the Maryland Tax Court within 30 days of the board's order. The SDAT office for the county is reached at 301-815-5350.

The county also lists a Senior Tax Credit of 20 percent of net county real property taxes for owners 65 or older who meet income limits, and a Homestead Tax Credit that limits yearly increases on a principal residence.

What historic district and code rules affect a Frederick seller?

In the city of Frederick, exterior work on a designated site or a property in a Historic Preservation Overlay district needs a certificate of approval from the Historic Preservation Commission. The commission reviews exterior features only and does not consider interior layout.

  • Changes do not have to be visible from the street to need review. Routine maintenance and landscaping with no material effect are exempt.
  • The commission has 45 days to act on a complete application, and silence means approval unless the applicant agrees to more time.
  • A certificate expires after three years without a building or zoning permit, with one six-month extension available.
  • Decisions can be challenged in the Circuit Court for Frederick County within 30 days.

Properties outside the overlay can still face demolition review when a plan removes more than 25 percent of floor area, changes significant roof lines or moves the structure.

For rental condition, the county says complaints about properties inside the city go to city inspectors at 301-600-3825.

More questions about Frederick, MD Property Tax Guide

What is the property tax rate in Frederick, MD?

The fiscal 2025 state table shows 1.7382 per $100 of assessed value inside the city, made up of a 1.0077 county rate and a 0.7305 municipal rate. Rates are reset each year, so check the current notice.

When is Frederick property tax due?

September 30 for annual bills and the first installment, and December 31 for the second installment. Interest starts October 1 at 1 percent per month, and a 1 percent discount applies to July payments.

Who do I call about my Frederick property tax?

Call the Frederick County Treasury at 301-600-1111 for billing, and SDAT at 301-815-5350 for the assessed value. The Treasury is at 30 North Market Street, open 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays.

Does the Frederick Historic Preservation Commission review a house sale?

No, a sale itself does not require approval. Exterior work on a designated or overlay property does, and the commission has 45 days to act on a complete application.

Can I sell a Frederick house with back taxes?

Yes, unpaid tax can be paid from the closing proceeds by the title company. Ask the Treasury for a lien certificate or tax status report to see the exact amount before you set the closing date.
